examples: The pencil has a point.
Do not touch the point.
The star has five points.

more.def: The sharp, thin end of something.
examples: The point of the needle is very sharp.
The pencil broke at the point.
A star has five points.
We got a point.
She scored a point.
The game is tied by a point.

more.def: A unit used to keep score in a game or contest.
examples: Our team scored three points before the break.
You get one point for every right answer.
She won the game by two points.

easy.def: To show where something is with your finger.
examples: I point at the bird.
She pointed to the door.
Point to the moon.

more.def: To show where something is by holding out a finger or an object toward it.
examples: The guide pointed to the top of the cliff.
She pointed at the map to show where we were.
The arrow points north.

easy.def: People whose job is to keep a town safe.
examples: The police helped us.
Call the police.
A police car drove by.

more.def: A group of people whose job is to keep the public safe and to make sure laws are followed.
examples: The police helped the lost boy find his parents.
A police officer stopped the traffic so the children could cross.
The police station is next to the library.
It is polite to say "thank you."
The polite girl said "please."
Be polite to the bus driver.

more.def: Having good manners and showing respect for other people.
examples: The polite boy held the door open for everyone.
It is polite to wait until everyone is served before eating.
He wrote a polite letter to thank his aunt.

easy.def: Dirty things that hurt the air, water, or land.
examples: Smoke from cars makes pollution.
Pollution makes the air dirty.
We pick up trash to stop pollution.

more.def: Harmful or dirty things that spoil the air, water, or land.
examples: Pollution in the river made it unsafe for the fish.
Factories must work to cut down on pollution.
Noise pollution from the airport bothers the neighbors.
The poor family needed food.
They were poor, but happy.
The poor village had one school.

more.def: Having little money or few things.
examples: Long ago, a poor farmer found a magic bean.
Some poor families get help buying food.
The poor town had one old school.

easy.def: Used when you feel sorry for someone.
examples: Poor kitten, you are wet!
Poor baby is tired.
The poor bird hurt its wing.

more.def: Used to show that you feel sorry for someone.
examples: The poor puppy is shivering in the rain.
Poor Max had to stay home with a cold.
The poor kitten was stuck in the tree.
His writing is poor.
The poor light made it hard to read.
Poor weather ruined the picnic.

more.def: Of low quality or not good enough.
examples: The sound in the old theater was poor.
She got a poor grade because she did not study.
A poor harvest meant less food for the winter.
Soccer is a popular game.
This is a popular book.
Pizza is popular with kids.

more.def: Liked or enjoyed by many people.
examples: That song is so popular that everyone knows the words.
The beach is popular with tourists in summer.
She is popular because she is friendly to everyone.
It is possible to fly.
Is it possible to go?
Rain is possible.

more.def: Able to happen, be done or be true.
examples: It is possible to see the stars from here on a clear night.
Is it possible to finish before lunch?
Snow is possible tomorrow, but it may rain instead.

easy.def: The strength to make things happen.
examples: The wave had great power.
I used all my power to push.
Superheroes have special powers.

more.def: The ability or strength to do something or to make something happen.
examples: A hurricane has enough power to knock down trees.
Whales have great power in their tails.
The king had the power to make new laws.
The storm cut the power to our street.
Solar panels make power from sunlight.
We lost power, so I used a flashlight.

more.def: Energy, especially electricity, that is used to run machines and light buildings.
examples: The power went out in the whole city during the storm.
Windmills turn wind into power for homes.
A small battery gives power to the toy car.
